---
title: "Quiz: shape models"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. A shape is a vector of $n$ corresponding landmarks; the point distribution model is $\mathbf x \approx \bar{\mathbf x} + \Phi\mathbf b$.

---

**Q1.** Why must landmark $i$ be "the same point" on every training shape?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The model averages and compares shapes coordinate by coordinate. If landmark 7 is the index finger tip on one hand and the middle finger tip on another, the average and the covariance mix different anatomical points, and PCA reports the mix-up as a large "mode of variation".
:::

---

**Q2.** Which differences between two landmark sets does Procrustes alignment remove, and which does it keep?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It removes position (translation), size (scale) and orientation (rotation); usually not reflection. Everything else, the **shape**, remains, and shows up as the residual distances after the fit.
:::

---

**Q3.** The best fit of one landmark set onto another is $a = 0.6$, $b = 0.8$. Give the scale and the rotation angle.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Scale $\sqrt{0.36 + 0.64} = 1$, angle $\operatorname{atan2}(0.8, 0.6) = 53.1°$: a pure rotation.
:::

---

**Q4.** Why does generalised Procrustes need several rounds instead of one?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The shapes are aligned to the current mean, but the mean is computed from the aligned shapes: each depends on the other. Starting from one shape as the mean, align all, recompute the mean, align again; it settles in two or three rounds. (The mean is also renormalised each round, otherwise it could shrink or drift.)
:::

---

**Q5.** A mode of a shape model has eigenvalue $\lambda = 0.04$. Between which values may $b$ lie for a plausible shape?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$|b| \le 3\sqrt{0.04} = 0.6$: three standard deviations of that mode over the training set.
:::

---

**Q6.** Your shape model of 20 vertebrae has 50 landmarks. How many modes can have non-zero variance?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
At most $20 - 1 = 19$, although the vectors have 100 coordinates: 20 centred shapes span at most a 19-dimensional space.
:::

---

**Q7.** Without alignment, the first mode of your hand model moves the whole hand to the left and right. Why, and is that a problem?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The hands were photographed at different positions, and that variation is larger than the differences in shape, so PCA puts it first. It is a problem: the modes mix pose and shape, the percentages are dominated by pose, and a search with this model can produce hands that shift instead of deform. Align first.
:::

---

**Q8.** A linear shape model is trained on fingers that bend at a joint. Why may $b = \pm 3\sqrt{\lambda}$ give a finger that is too long?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A bending finger moves its tip along an arc. A linear mode moves it along a straight line (the chord direction); going far along the line leaves the arc and stretches the finger. A bend needs several linear modes, and extreme combinations of them give implausible shapes.
:::

---

**Q9.** *(math)* Why is $\mathbf b = \Phi^\top(\mathbf x - \bar{\mathbf x})$ the best $\mathbf b$ for a given shape $\mathbf x$?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The columns of $\Phi$ are orthonormal, so $\bar{\mathbf x} + \Phi\mathbf b$ is closest to $\mathbf x$ (least squares) when $\Phi\mathbf b$ is the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf x - \bar{\mathbf x}$ onto the span of the modes, i.e. $\mathbf b = \Phi^\top(\mathbf x - \bar{\mathbf x})$: a change of basis, as for the DFT or the PCA scores.
:::
